newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army says it regrouping for counter-attack.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army says it regrouping for counter-attack.

text.p: Zaire's rag-tag army, driven from its eastern provinces by a coalition of Tutsi and other rebels, is regrouping 300 km (190 miles) from the battle zone for a counter-attack, military sources say.

"The soldiers who retreated from Bukavu and Goma have been sent to Kindu, where they are being prepared for the assault, although of course we cannot say when that will come," one senior officer told Reuters on Saturday.

Earlier, Army Chief of Staff General Eluki Monga said he now had the means to recapture those parts of east Zaire in rebel hands. "We have lost the battle, not the war," state radio quoted him as saying.
Estimates of the size of the army range from 25,000 to over 50,000 but some military sources say numbers have been inflated in the past to increase the budgets of commanders.
The revolt in the east is the latest manifestation of pressures threatening to tear apart the sprawling, chaotic and corruption-plagued former Belgian colony.

Earlier this month, Eluki accused the government of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo of not giving the army the means to defend the country against the rebels, a coalition of opponents of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The radio quoted Eluki, who was himself in the east, as saying the government had now put everything at the disposal of the army for it to recapture the lost territory.
Kindu is the closest major outpost to the fighting, although roads linking it with Bukavu are almost impassable.
The defeated soldiers mostly headed for Kisangani, 500 km (310 miles) away, in commandeered vehicles, leaving a trail of looting and destruction in their wake.

Reports from Kisangani, once mooted as a staging post in the international operation to feed and protect Hutu refugees fleeing the fighting, say soldiers continue to arrive there, some of them having walked part of the way.
Other deserters were arrested on the outskirts of Kinshasa, having floated down the Zaire River on commandeered barges.
At present the main resistance to the rebels comes from Hutu hardliners blamed for the 1994 genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis and their sympathisers in Rwanda.

Hundreds of thousands of Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals are flooding home but journalists reported fighting in the lush hills west of the deserted Lac Vert refugee camp near Goma on Saturday as rebels pursued the Hutu fighters deeper into Zaire.
The Hutu fighters -- ex-Rwandan army soldiers and members of the dreaded Interahamwe militia -- fled into the bush to escape a relentless bombardment by Zairean rebels earlier in the week.
Zairean soldiers have long since fled the area but a range of Zaireans from students who staged anti-Kengo street protests to politicians are rallying behind the army.

Zaire's deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka, speaking in Brussels on Friday, accused neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi's Tutsi-dominated armies of occupying the eastern towns of Uvira, Bukavu and Goma. "We are determined to wage a total war...We have the means," he said.
Traditional celebrations to mark National Army Day, which usually include military parades, were cancelled on Saturday.
"We are in a state of war," an army spokesman said.
